Why Emergency Food?

Whether you're a serious prepper or just want peace of mind during storm season, a freeze-dried emergency food supply is the easiest way to ensure your family eats when grocery stores are empty or the power is out. No refrigeration needed, no complicated prep — just add water and wait a few minutes.

The two heavyweights in this space are Ready Hour's 120-Serving Entree Bucket and Mountain House's Classic Assortment Bucket. Both are made in the USA, both boast 25+ year shelf lives, and both have rabid fan bases. But they target very different buyers. Here's the full breakdown.

📦 Servings & Volume Showdown

Ready Hour 120-Serving Entree Bucket

This is where Ready Hour absolutely dominates. At 120 total servings spread across 22 resealable pouches, this bucket is designed for serious emergency preparedness. Each pouch contains multiple servings, so you can open one pouch, use what you need, and reseal the rest. At $1.17 per serving, this is the most cost-effective entree bucket in its class — period.

The 22-pouch variety includes classic comfort foods like Chicken Alfredo Pasta, Creamy Pasta & Vegetables, Teriyaki Rice, and Cheesy Macaroni. These aren't just survival rations — they're meals you'd actually eat around the campfire or during a power outage. The bucket itself is flood-safe with a sturdy handle, making it easy to grab and go if you need to evacuate.

Mountain House Classic Bucket

Mountain House takes a different approach: quality over quantity. Their Classic Bucket contains 24 total servings across 8 pouches — a mix of breakfast and dinner entrees. You'll find Lasagna with Meat Sauce, Scrambled Eggs with Bacon, Chicken Teriyaki, and Beef Stroganoff — real meals from a brand that's been freeze-drying food since 1969.

At $3.75 per serving, Mountain House costs more than three times as much per meal. But those servings are bigger — each pouch of Mountain House is a generous portion, and the flavor is widely considered the best in the industry. This bucket is better for short-term emergencies, camping trips, or smaller households where 24 servings go a long way.

👅 Taste & Quality

Let's be honest — you're buying emergency food because you might need it, but you'll actually use it more if it tastes good.

Mountain House: The Taste King

Mountain House has been perfecting freeze-dried meals for over 50 years, and it shows. Their 30-Year Taste Guarantee isn't just marketing — they genuinely believe their food tastes great even after decades of storage. The Scrambled Eggs with Bacon is legendary (it actually tastes like real eggs and real bacon). The Lasagna has actual pasta, meat sauce, and cheese that rehydrates perfectly. Reviewers consistently rate Mountain House at 4.8 stars — the highest in the category.

The secret? Mountain House uses a proprietary freeze-drying process that preserves the cellular structure of ingredients. When you add hot water, the food rehydrates to near-fresh texture. No mush, no weird aftertaste.

Ready Hour: Solid, Honest Flavors

Ready Hour's food is good — not great, but genuinely good. At 4.4 stars, reviewers consistently say things like "tastes better than I expected for emergency food" and "actually pretty good, especially for the price." The Chicken Alfredo and Cheesy Macaroni are fan favorites. The Teriyaki Rice has a pleasant sweetness that stands out from typical survival fare.

Where Ready Hour trails Mountain House is in texture and refinement. The rehydration takes longer (15-20 minutes vs Mountain House's 8-10), and the finished texture is slightly more porridge-like. But for 1/3 the cost per serving? Most people happily make that trade.

🕐 Shelf Life & Storage

Both buckets are designed to be set-and-forget emergency supplies:

  • Ready Hour: 25-year shelf life in cool, dry storage. The flood-safe bucket with gasket lid adds an extra layer of protection against moisture and pests.
  • Mountain House: 30-year taste guarantee. The #10 can-style pouches are nitrogen-flushed for maximum preservation. Slightly longer shelf life, but the standard bucket is less weather-resistant.

Both require cool, dry storage — think basement, pantry, or a closet away from heat sources. Neither requires refrigeration. Both are designed to survive in a garage or shed, but extreme temperature swings will shorten any food's shelf life.

One advantage of Ready Hour that doesn't get enough attention: the resealable pouches. Mountain House's Classic Bucket pouches are single-use — once you open one, you need to eat the whole thing (or refrigerate leftovers for a day or two). Ready Hour's pouches reseal and last up to a year after opening, which is huge for households that want to rotate through their supply gradually.

💰 Value Breakdown

Here's the math that matters:

  • Ready Hour 120-Serving: $139.99 = $1.17/serving. 120 total meals, 22 pouches, resealable, flood-safe bucket.
  • Mountain House Classic: $89.99 = $3.75/serving. 24 total meals, 8 pouches, superior taste, longer shelf life.

If you're feeding a family of 4 for a week, the Ready Hour bucket wins by a landslide — you get 5x the servings for only 1.56x the price. That's 120 servings vs 24. One Ready Hour bucket could last a family of 4 a full week of three meals a day, with leftovers.

If you're a solo prepper, a couple, or someone who primarily wants emergency food for camping and occasional use, the Mountain House bucket is the better value despite the higher per-serving cost. The taste difference matters more when you're eating it by choice around a campfire, and you won't be staring at a giant bucket that takes years to rotate through.

🎒 Portability & Ease of Use

Ready Hour

The Ready Hour bucket comes with a built-in handle and a flood-safe sealing lid. This is a genuine advantage for emergency scenarios — if you need to evacuate, you grab the bucket by the handle and go. Each pouch inside is labeled, and the instructions are clearly printed. Preparation requires a pot and heat source — add water, bring to a boil, simmer 15-20 minutes, and eat. It's simple but requires cookware and fuel.

Mountain House

Mountain House's preparation is the gold standard for simplicity. Just boil water, pour it into the pouch (yes, the pouch itself is the bowl), stir, wait 8-10 minutes, and eat directly from the pouch. No pot to clean, no plates needed. This makes Mountain House significantly more practical for camping, backpacking, or situations where fuel and water are limited. The trade-off is no handle on the bucket and a less weather-resistant container.

🏆 The Verdict

Our Pick: Ready Hour 120-Serving Entree Bucket

Both buckets are excellent, and honestly, your ideal choice depends entirely on who you're feeding and why.

Choose Ready Hour 120-Serving if:

  • You're stocking for a family — 120 servings goes a long way
  • Budget per serving is your primary concern — $1.17/serving is unbeatable
  • You want resealable pouches for gradual use and rotation
  • A flood-safe, grab-and-go bucket matters for your storage setup
  • You're preparing for extended emergencies (weeks, not days)

Choose Mountain House Classic Bucket if:

  • Taste is your top priority — Mountain House is the industry standard bearer
  • You're a smaller household (1-2 people) who won't need 120 servings
  • You want eat-from-pouch convenience for camping and backpacking
  • The 30-year taste guarantee gives you peace of mind for long-term storage
  • You prefer quicker prep time — 8 minutes vs 20 minutes matters in an emergency

For most families, the Ready Hour 120-Serving Entree Bucket is the better investment. At $1.17 per serving with resealable pouches and a flood-safe bucket, it's purpose-built for real emergency preparedness at a price that won't break the bank. You can feed a family of four for a week for roughly the cost of two takeout dinners. That's preparedness anyone can afford.
